candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the XML document bytes/characters supplied to any parsing entry point (XmlMapper.readValue(..., type), XmlFactory.createParser(InputStream/Reader/byte[]/char[]/String)). Element/attribute text of the parsed document becomes the deserialized values, and any DOCTYPE/entity declarations in that document are processed by the underlying XMLStreamReader.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that _initFactories only sets output namespace repairing and input coalescing (lines 138-141) - no security properties anywhere in the repository (grep for DTD/entity/security found no handling in src/main). Confirmed the factory is used unmodified at every parse entry point (lines 536, 554, 575, 593). Confirmed XmlFactory exposes XMLInputFactory injection/override (constructors lines 90-102; getters/setters lines 336-351), so callers *can* harden it - meaning impact is configuration/provider dependent, not universal. pom.xml has stax-api provided and woodstox-core only test-scoped (pom.xml lines 67-94), so production deployments may use the JDK provider whose defaults are entity-processing. No runtime/reproduction was performed (source review only) and I could not consult upstream history/CVE data offline to confirm whether and when a fix landed.
candidates.impact: Confidentiality: disclosure of arbitrary files readable by the process (e.g., configuration/credential files) by placing the file content into a mapped String value (classic XXE). Also SSRF: entities/DTD references can cause the server to request attacker-chosen internal URLs ('external parameter entities' / external DTD), reaching services not otherwise exposed. Availability: entity-expansion ('billion laughs'-style) documents can consume CPU/memory when the provider has no expansion limits. All of this occurs during normal XmlMapper deserialization of untrusted XML.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses XmlMapper/XmlFactory defaults (no caller-supplied hardened XMLInputFactory and no call to XMLInputFactory.setProperty on the default factory); the runtime Stax provider resolves external entities (the JDK's built-in XMLInputFactory implementation defaults SUPPORT_DTD and IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES to true; Woodstox, recommended in README and present here only at test scope, behaves differently); the application parses untrusted XML; the process can reach the entity target (local file, internal URL).
candidates.root_cause: XmlFactory's protected constructor creates the parser with the unconfigured default provider (XMLInputFactory.newInstance(), line 113) and _initFactories() only sets IS_COALESCING and IS_REPAIRING_NAMESPACES; it never sets XMLInputFactory.SUPPORT_DTD=false or XMLInputFactory.IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false. The resulting factory is then used verbatim by all _createParser(...) variants, so DTD/external-entity handling is left at the Stax provider's defaults.
candidates.title: XmlFactory/XmlMapper default Stax configuration allows XML External Entity (XXE) processing
candidates.trace: new XmlMapper() -> new XmlFactory() [XmlMapper.java:48-49] -> XmlFactory protected constructor -> XMLInputFactory.newInstance() [XmlFactory.java:113] -> _initFactories() sets only IS_COALESCING [XmlFactory.java:141] -> parsed via _createParser(): _xmlInputFactory.createXMLStreamReader(in/reader/arrays) [XmlFactory.java:536,554,575,593] -> FromXmlParser/XmlTokenStream iterate the reader [XmlTokenStream.java:350-371, 374-388]. Because DTD support and external-entity resolution were never disabled, a document such as a DOCTYPE declaring an external SYSTEM entity is resolved by the provider and the resolved text is surfaced as the parsed value/attribute text, i.e., attacker XML is transformed into local-file or remote resource content inside the mapped object.
candidates.unverified: The actual XMLInputFactory implementation present in a given deployment (JDK SJSXP vs Woodstox vs Aalto) and its concrete entity/DTD defaults; the exact externally-observable result (file content vs exception) for a specific payload; whether upstream (or this benchmark's fix commit) addressed this exact configuration, and whether the curated case targets this issue rather than another XmlFactory concern. No test execution was permitted, so runtime exploitation is not confirmed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-611 Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference (XXE) / CWE-776 entity expansion

coverage_summary: Source scope: 90 files at root, 89 model-visible (86 Java + pom.xml + README.md + .travis.yml); 1 file excluded by the environment's sensitive-name filter and therefore not reviewed. P1 relation index: 86 Java files parsed (0 parse errors), 1470 symbols, 3043 call relations, 2562 edges, 4 named facts; 12 files omitted from the index (non-Java/no symbols) and the index explicitly supports no control-flow or data-flow analysis, with 2232 unresolved calls - index labels were treated only as navigation hints and every cited location was verified against source text. I reviewed all main product sources (XmlFactory, XmlMapper, FromXmlParser, XmlTokenStream, XmlReadContext, ElementWrapper, WrapperHandlingDeserializer, XmlBeanDeserializerModifier, XmlTextDeserializer, ToXmlGenerator, XmlBeanSerializer*, XmlSerializerProvider, UnwrappingXmlBeanSerializer, XmlBeanPropertyWriter, JacksonXmlAnnotationIntrospector, XmlAnnotationIntrospector, JacksonXmlModule, XmlTypeResolverBuilder, XmlRootNameLookup, StaxUtil, AnnotationUtil, TypeUtil, XmlInfo, DefaultXmlPrettyPrinter, annotations) and used the test tree, pom.xml and README for configuration/context. No execution, build, or dynamic analysis was performed.
limitations: Source-only review: no code execution, dependency resolution, or exploit verification was permitted, so all behavior described is inferred from code and Java/Stax defaults.

The concrete impact of the XmlFactory finding depends on the Stax provider present at runtime (JDK built-in vs Woodstox/Aalto); the pom's test-scoped Woodstox means the repository's own test environment may not reproduce file-disclosure XXE, and I could not test this.
One repository file is hidden by the environment's sensitive-name filter and could not be inspected; it may contain project metadata relevant to the case.
The P1 index provides only syntactic navigation (no data/control flow, no semantic resolution), so reachability and exploitability of the candidate were argued from source text, not proven.

I could not consult upstream release notes, CVE data, or the fix commit offline, so I cannot state which specific upstream change (if any) corresponds to this snapshot or whether a different curated issue is the intended target.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlFactory JDK-deserialization sink: readResolve() calls Class.forName(_jdkXmlInFactory).newInstance() and Class.forName(_jdkXmlOutFactory).newInstance() on class names supplied by the serialized stream (XmlFactory.java:190-194, read via readObject() at 208-214).
rejected_leads.reason: Concrete attacker-controlled class-name sink, but it only matters when an application JDK-deserializes untrusted data containing an XmlFactory/XmlMapper (an already catastrophic trust boundary), the result is coerced to XMLInputFactory/XMLOutputFactory, and the effect is primarily arbitrary no-arg instantiation. It is a weak gadget rather than a practical library vulnerability, and no source evidence shows this path is reachable from ordinary XML input.

rejected_leads.lead: Parser/generator feature mix-up: all XmlFactory._createParser(...) variants pass _generatorFeatures/_xmlGeneratorFeatures into FromXmlParser instead of _parserFeatures/_xmlParserFeatures (XmlFactory.java:541-542, 559-560, 580-581, 598-599).
rejected_leads.reason: Real configuration bug (parser JsonParser.Features are ignored/misapplied and generator feature bits collide with parser bits), but the affected flags are not consumed by FromXmlParser and no confidentiality/integrity/availability impact could be demonstrated from source; looks like a correctness bug, not a vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded parsing resources (no nesting/size/entity limits in FromXmlParser/XmlTokenStream; _initializeXmlReader() loops until START_ELEMENT at XmlFactory.java:645-652).
rejected_leads.reason: Generic hardening/DoS concerns with no concrete attacker-triggered defect proven in this snapshot; the loop terminates per Stax contract and limits are normally the provider's or databind's responsibility.

rejected_leads.lead: Serialization-side XML injection via attacker-influenced element/attribute names (ToXmlGenerator.setNextName/writeFieldName).
rejected_leads.reason: Names are ultimately written through Stax writer APIs (writeStartElement/writeAttribute), which validate/escape names and text; no raw concatenation path (writeRaw is only used by the pretty-printer for fixed whitespace) was found.

summary: Snapshot is FasterXML jackson-dataformat-xml 2.7.4-SNAPSHOT (86 Java files, jackson-core/databind 2.7.3, Stax API provided, Woodstox only test-scoped). I read the core product sources end-to-end (XmlFactory, XmlMapper, FromXmlParser, XmlTokenStream, XmlReadContext, ElementWrapper, deser modifiers/deserializers, ToXmlGenerator, serializer/provider/bean-serializer classes, StaxUtil/AnnotationUtil/TypeUtil/XmlInfo/XmlRootNameLookup/DefaultXmlPrettyPrinter) and used tests/pom/README for context. The single strongest security issue is a default-insecure XML parsing configuration in XmlFactory: the parser factory created via XMLInputFactory.newInstance() is never hardened against DTD/external-entity processing (the only security-relevant setup is IS_COALESCING), so an XmlMapper built with defaults parses attacker-supplied XML with whatever entity-processing defaults the runtime Stax provider has (JDK's provider defaults to SUPPORT_DTD=true / IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=true), enabling classic XXE/entity-expansion attacks. No code in the repository disables DTDs or entity resolution, and no in-repo documentation warns about it. I rejected other leads (JDK-deserialization Class.forName in readResolve, parser/generator feature mix-up in _createParser) as weaker/less security-impactful.
